turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brought you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, doctor, what brings me in is... I just can't get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. It's like every time I have to deal with a banker or someone from the county, I feel like they're just staring at all the cracks, the sun spots, the sagging skin. My wife tells me I just look like a man who's worked outdoors his whole life, but I can't stop focusing on it. It just really bothers me.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an inability to stop focusing on perceived flaws in his skin and appearance (cracks, spots, sagging) despite his wife reassuring him they are normal for outdoor work.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself spending a lot of time each day checking your skin in mirrors, trying to cover it up, or picking at it because of how it looks?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I do spend a lot of time on it. Especially before I have to go somewhere important, like a loan meeting or setting up a table at a craft fair. I'll catch myself checking the bathroom mirror, and then I'll check the truck mirror again before I drive off. I just keep... well, turning my hat this way and that, trying to see how my face looks in the light. 

And I look at my hands constantly, comparing them to the younger workers we have around the place. I end up doing all that checking and adjusting until I realize I've just wasted a good chunk of time that I really should be using out on the farm.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient explicitly confirms engaging in time-consuming, repetitive appearance-related behaviors, including repeatedly checking mirrors, adjusting their hat, and comparing their hands to others.

turns.doctor_question: Even when you're alone at home and no one else is around, do you still find yourself worrying about how your face and hands look, or does that worry only come up when you know you'll be around other people?
turns.patient_response: Well, it's definitely worse when I have to go into town or meet with people, but... yeah, even when I'm just out in the fields or sitting in the house, it's still there. I'll be watching TV or eating dinner, and I'll catch sight of my hands, and I just start thinking about how old and worn out they look. Or I'll walk past the mirror in the hall and just stop to look at my face. So, I guess I'm still worrying about it even when it's just me and my wife at home. It just doesn't really go away.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent worry and preoccupation with the appearance of his hands and face that persists even when alone and 'doesn't really go away'.
symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient reports appearance-related mirror checking, noting that he stops to examine his face whenever he walks past the hall mirror.

turns.doctor_question: When your wife or others tell you that your skin just looks like a typical outdoorsman's, do you think there's a chance they might be right, or do you feel certain that your skin really is as flawed as you perceive it to be?
turns.patient_response: Well, I hear what she's saying, and I know she means well, but... I just can't see it that way. When I look in the mirror, all I see are those deep cracks and the spots. It doesn't look like just normal weathering to me. It looks... bad. So, no, I don't really think they're right. I feel pretty certain that it looks exactly as awful as I think it does.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from your concerns about your skin, do you ever feel that people are talking about you, watching you, or trying to harm you in other ways?
turns.patient_response: No, I don't feel anything like that. I mean, I worry about people noticing my skin when I'm in town, like I said, but I don't think anyone is out to get me or watching my every move or anything. It's just the skin stuff that bothers me. I don't have any worries about people trying to harm me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies believing that people are out to get them, watching their every move, or trying to harm them, ruling out persecutory or referential delusions.
